sm: Mindy Tate, CEO of Franklin Tomorrow, opens this FrankTalks event at VFW Post 4893 in Franklin by leading the Pledge of Allegiance and explaining that the morning is about learning about veterans organizations and meeting veterans. She thanks the program's partners and mentions that the group is planning locations and topics for next year. A representative of Williamson Health speaks, noting he is the son of two Vietnam combat nurses. A video from Doctor Devin Sherman explains that November is Lung Cancer Awareness Month, that lung cancer is hard to detect, and that screening targets smokers aged 50 to 75 who smoke or quit within fifteen years.

Williamson Health is offering a low dose CT lung scan to anyone for one hundred fifty dollars, regardless of risk or insurance coverage. After a humorous college football video from a partner bank, Mindy hands the floor to Tim, the commander of VFW Post 4893. He is an Air Force Reserve veteran who served in Iraq. He explains that the Veterans of Foreign Wars was founded in 1899 by Spanish American War veterans and helped establish the VA, the post 9/11 GI Bill, and the PACT Act. The post was founded in 1945 and named for Second Lieutenant Roy Alley, a Pacific bombardier.

Tim says Lieutenant Alley died when his plane went down and is buried in the Manila American Cemetery. Full VFW membership requires an honorable discharge and overseas conflict service. He tours the post's murals and artifacts, including a guitar made in Vietnam that was carried by a soldier, a shadow box from the National Guard's Task Force Phoenix in Memphis, and a piece of the Berlin Wall. The post judges the Voice of Democracy student contest, hosts Guitars for Vets, and lets American Legion Posts 215 and 22 meet there. It will share a parade float with the Elks, does not allow smoking inside, and holds public events like a recent music festival with eleven bands.

Tim describes the post's Musical Showcase, where writers with military connections play songs, and encourages people to check the Facebook page. Associate membership for supporters costs fifty dollars a year and is good for all of next calendar year if you join now. The post is also restarting its auxiliary for close relatives of eligible veterans, which folded about a decade ago. He mentions poppy donations and QR codes for giving, and all veterans in the room raise their hands. Bob, a Navy submariner who served six years, then takes over and introduces Don Lane, chairman of the Williamson County African American Veterans Foundation.

Don Lane, a longtime American Legion member and vice commander of Post 215, thanks Bob for championing a museum to honor Black veterans. Bob explains that the foundation, a nonprofit with nine board members, began as a memorial garden for the late Robert Mac McMillan. Contractors then found the building badly deteriorated. Post 215 was founded in 1946 by three World War Two veterans, including Tuskegee Airman Robert Murdock, and bought its building in 1952, encasing a 1915 house in cinder block. He recounts local Black military history, including Sergeant George Jordan, the county's only Medal of Honor recipient, and the Caruthers family's sacrifices. The building also served as a community center and had leaky ceilings and failing air conditioning.

Bob says the building was gutted and rebuilt with community help, and it will become both Post 215 and a museum telling the story of African American veterans, with thirteen display panels. A grand reopening is hoped for early 2027, and fundraising continues, including for an endowment. Seth Ford, a member of several veterans groups and a political action committee called Honor Our Veterans, says Williamson County is lucky to have so many veteran organizations and urges younger veterans to get involved and ask older members for coffee. Mindy mentions the Williamson Herald's Salute to Veterans and asks people to thank veterans. Tom Lawrence, parade chairman for twenty five years, begins explaining why the Veterans Day parade was revived in 2001.

Tom Lawrence says the parade had not been held since 1946 before it returned in 2001 after a wave of patriotism. This year's parade starts at 11 a.m. sharp on Wednesday, preceded by a veterans brunch at the archives, with bells tolling and a flyover beforehand. He expects about five thousand spectators, around a thousand veterans, and a hundred to a hundred fifty classic cars carrying veterans. Every fourth grader in the Franklin Special School District marches, and this year all the high school bands are participating. The route runs up Main Street around the square and up Third Avenue to Bicentennial Park, and the parade uses sixty three school buses.

The group learns that only twelve World War Two veterans are believed to be alive in Williamson County. Grand marshals include Vietnam veteran Art Jacobs, Navy nurse Beverly Williams, and Ben Welch, the former county veterans service officer. David Tooth man is the new service officer, and a younger chairman will replace Tom next year alongside Monique McCullough. Mindy closes by stressing civic pride, urging people to fly flags on Veterans Day and support the Legion foundation, the VFW post and the parade. The next event is the second Monday in December at Columbia State, with coffee at nine and the program at nine thirty. In answer to a question, a speaker explains that the VFW additionally requires foreign conflict service, and Mindy thanks the post for hosting without a rental fee.
